Which department decided that residents cannot return to Wang Fuk Court?

Multiple owners raised related issues during the Q&A session. At least five questioners asked Hop On, the property management company, which department decided that residents currently cannot return to Wang Fuk Court, and what was the legal basis for the lockdown? Hop On initially did not give a direct answer on the first four occasions, only saying that Wang Fuk Court remains sealed off and that arranging access is beyond the scope of the management company's authority. They also advised residents in need to contact the dedicated social worker assigned to each household, which at one point triggered an uproar among owners from several estates.

Hop On unaware of legal basis on which authorities imposed lockdown

Solicitor Leung Ping-chiu finally responded that Hop On is unaware of the legal basis on which the authorities imposed the lockdown, and it would be inappropriate for the company to explain on their behalf to avoid misinterpreting the government's considerations. As for the much-anticipated survey reports on the remaining seven blocks of Wang Fuk Court, Hop On said the typhoon and rainy seasons are approaching, and the findings may be released once the authorities complete their surveys. Hop On also said that after seeking legal advice, it considers the demand to go beyond its responsibilities as the property manager.

Owners question whether government will reclaim ownership via donations and skip rebuilding to save compensation for China Taiping?

The government previously stated it would not rebuild on the original site. At the meeting, several owners questioned whether this meant the HK$2 billion "fire insurance" payout calculated based on the cost of restoring the building structure would not be honoured, asking: "Is the government reclaiming ownership through donations without rebuilding so as to save China Taiping the compensation?" Ms Lau, a representative of China Taiping Insurance (Hong Kong), said that once policy liability is established, the company will pay out according to the policy terms regardless of whether repairs or rebuilding are undertaken, and that the acquisition would not affect policy liability or the calculation of the amount. However, Ms Lau also said that a further assessment of the specific policy and legal liability can only be made after the independent committee and relevant government departments complete their investigations and publish their findings.

Repair of Wang Chi House estimated at HK$30 million

Hop On also gave an update on Wang Chi House, which was unaffected by the fire. The company had previously estimated that repairs to Wang Chi House would cost at least HK$30 million and take at least nine months, involving re-tiling of external walls, electrical repairs, and other works. At today's meeting, Hop On revised the total to about HK$32 million, with a construction period of three to nine months. Solicitor Leung Ping-chiu, invited by Hop On to attend the meeting, pointed out that Wang Chi House forms part of the entire estate under the Deed of Mutual Covenant. Handling it independently would require substantial amendments to the DMC with the agreement of all owners—a complex and costly procedure.

Owners question Hop On for failing to convene owners' meeting within statutory deadline on the grounds that contacting owners was time-consuming, yet successfully issuing subsidy cheques on behalf of the URA earlier this year; ask: 'What's so difficult that you can't even get us owners together for a meeting?' Meeting chairperson and Hop On Property Services Director Chan Wai-kwong did not give a direct answer, saying it was a venue issue, and that finding a venue capable of accommodating a thousand people as requested by residents was extremely difficult. Ultimately, the Home Affairs Department had to provide the venue before the meeting could proceed. Some owners criticised the explanation as unreasonable: "Hong Kong hosts so many mega events and can easily stage a show for tens of thousands of people in a single venue—yet you tell me there's not one venue that can fit our 2,000. That's really hard to accept. I hope you won't use this as an excuse any longer."
